$comment: Passenger demand profiles by building type. See docs/03-traffic-and-statistics.md.

arrivalProcess.$comment: Passengers arrive in groups, not singly. Batch size materially changes loading and stop patterns.

profiles.name: Prestige office
profiles.blurb: The morning crush at a headline address: nearly everyone pours in through the lobby at once, and the bank is judged on how fast that queue clears.

profiles.name: Standard office
profiles.blurb: An ordinary office morning: a steady stream in through the lobby, with light floor-to-floor errands once people are at their desks.

profiles.name: Residential
profiles.blurb: Apartment mornings run downward — residents leave through the lobby, and families ride together, so groups are larger. Evenings invert to an up-peak.
profiles.$comment: PM inverts to up-peak. Larger batches: families travel together.

profiles.name: Hotel
profiles.blurb: Hotel demand runs both ways all day: guests come and go while housekeeping and room service move between floors, with no single dominant direction.

profiles.name: Hospital
profiles.blurb: A hospital never empties. People move both ways all day, the busiest moments are shift changes rather than a morning rush, and a bed needs a car of its own.
profiles.$comment: CITED: CIBSE Guide D groups hospitals with the buildings whose demand is two-way and whose quality-of-service target is looser than an office's -- Guide D's recommended interval band for hospital passenger lifts is 40-60 s against 25-30 s for offices, and 50 s is the middle of it. DERIVED, not quoted from a table: arrivalRatePctPop5min. Guide D gives hospital handling capacity in beds and departments rather than as a percentage of an occupant population, so the 6-11% band is set from this project's own convention -- below an office's 11-15% because a hospital's peak is a shift change involving staff rather than the whole building arriving, and above residential's 3-7% because the building is busy all day rather than twice. NOT CITED, and stated as an assumption: the 35/35/30 split. The interfloor share is the highest of any profile here because porters, clinicians and diagnostics traffic move between floors without touching the entrance, and that is the characteristic this profile exists to express; it is the number most worth measuring against a real building. LIMITATION: one profile cannot express that a bed journey and a visitor journey have different service expectations. The building distinguishes them by BANK (st-jude-hospital's bed bank carries 5000 lb cars at a 3.0 s transfer), not here.

demandTemplates.name: CIBSE rise-and-fall template
demandTemplates.shape: ramp up to peak, hold, ramp down
demandTemplates.$comment: Use this. Each replication generates an independent passenger set, satisfying the independence condition required for confidence intervals. CLOCK (startOfDayMin 510 = 08:30). CITED: that a morning up-peak is a design case, and its demand level -- CIBSE Guide D tabulates the up-peak in %pop/5min. NOT CITED: the hour. Guide D and ISO 8100-32 tabulate design PEAKS, not clocks, and no table in this project's reference set publishes an hour of day for one. DERIVED: 08:30, by placing the template's HOLD rather than its start. The hold is the reported five minutes and sits centred in the 30-minute run, at +12.5 to +17.5 min, so a start of 08:30 puts the reported peak at 08:42:30-08:47:30, centred on 08:45 -- the conventional office arrival peak. The start reads as a derived consequence rather than a chosen round number, and that is the intended reading. LIMITATION: the derivation is a function of durationMin and of the 5-minute hold, so changing either leaves 08:30 no longer centring the hold on 08:45, and nothing in the code will say so. Nothing statistical reads startOfDayMin today -- intensityAt, splitAt and integratedIntensityS never see it, and packages/core/src/traffic/dayStartIdentity.test.ts holds every shipped trace byte-identical with and without it -- so the assumption is free. It stops being free the moment a phase boundary becomes a measurement boundary. DECISIONS.md section D244.

demandTemplates.name: ISO 8100-32 constant demand
demandTemplates.$comment: Single long run. Incompatible with confidence intervals across replications because waiting times within one run are correlated. Supported for cross-checking only. NO CLOCK, and the absence is a declaration rather than an oversight: `startOfDayMin` is deliberately omitted because ISO's constant demand is a rate held long enough to cross-check an analytical baseline, not a time of day. Omission means 'this template has no hour', never 'its hour is midnight' -- a 0 here would be an invented clock, and a presentation layer reading one would draw a two-hour run at 00:00. This is the only shipped template without an hour. DECISIONS.md section D244.

demandTemplates.name: CIBSE Guide D lunch two-way template
demandTemplates.shape: the rise-and-fall intensity, with the directional mix swinging from outgoing-dominant to incoming-dominant across the period
demandTemplates.$comment: The lunch mixed peak: occupants ride down to the terminal to leave the building, and later ride up again on their return, so the SAME period is outgoing-dominant early and incoming-dominant late. CITED: the period's mix is 45% incoming / 45% outgoing / 10% interfloor (CIBSE Guide D, 2010, carried into 2020; the same split is what BCO Guide to Specification 2014 pairs with a 13%/5min lunchtime two-way demand). Alternatives in the literature are 40/40/20 (Barney 2003a) and 42/42/16 (BCO 2009); the CIBSE figure is taken because Guide D is this project's primary reference. DERIVED, and not quoted from any table: the two endpoints. At the instant the period opens nobody has returned yet, so incoming is 0; interfloor is held at the cited 10% throughout; the mix is linear in time and symmetric about the midpoint, so its time-average is (start+end)/2 = 45/45/10 exactly -- the cited figure is REPRODUCED by the endpoints rather than assumed beside them. NOT CITED, and inherited rather than invented: every geometric number here. durationMin, the 5-minute hold and the zero baseline are the rise-and-fall record's own, so this template adds no uncited duration. LIMITATION: an endpoint of exactly 0 incoming is the widest arc consistent with the cited mean, and a measured building's arc is smoother at its ends; `traffic.lunchTwoWay.mixAmplitude` scales the arc about that mean, and 0 collapses it to a flat 45/45/10 at identical total demand. CLOCK (startOfDayMin 735 = 12:15). CITED: that a lunch two-way period is a design case, and its demand level and mix, both above. NOT CITED: the hour -- Guide D gives the lunch two-way as a design case and publishes no time of day for it. DERIVED: 12:15, by placing the period's MIDPOINT rather than its start. The midpoint is the one instant this template names in its own right -- the mix crossover, where outgoing and incoming are equal at the cited 45/45/10 and the intensity is at its peak -- and putting that at 12:30 gives a 12:15-12:45 period. LIMITATION: as for rise-and-fall, the derivation is a function of durationMin, and nothing statistical reads the hour today; note also that shiftTemplatePeak moves the crossover within the period while leaving startOfDayMin alone, so a shifted run still began at 12:15 and no longer crosses over at 12:30. DECISIONS.md section D244.

demandTemplates.name: Shift-change template
demandTemplates.shape: two interior peaks separated by a trough, with demand never reaching zero
demandTemplates.$comment: The pattern a hospital, a factory or a call centre actually runs, and the one shape no existing template can express: TWO peaks inside one period. `rise-and-fall` has a single interior maximum and `constant-iso` has none, so a run that wants 'the outgoing shift leaves while the incoming shift arrives, twice' had to be approximated by a wider single peak, which is a different question -- it spreads the same demand instead of concentrating it twice. DERIVED, not cited: the geometry. The 30-minute duration and the full-run report window are `lunch-two-way`'s, inherited so this template adds no uncited duration; the two peaks sit at 1/4 and 3/4 of the period and the trough between them holds at a NON-ZERO baseline, because the defining fact about a shift change is that the building is still occupied between them. NOT CITED: the peak-to-trough ratio. There is no Guide D table for it, and it is stated as an assumption rather than a measurement. LIMITATION: the two peaks are equal. A real shift change is asymmetric -- more people leave at the end of a day shift than arrive for a night one -- and expressing that needs a directional arc like `lunch-two-way`'s, which this template deliberately does not carry so that the two features can be measured apart. CLOCK (startOfDayMin 885 = 14:45). NOT CITED, and this one is an assumption end to end rather than a derived placement of a cited period: no source in this project's reference set publishes shift changeover hours, and real ones vary by industry and by site. The period is placed by its MIDPOINT -- the trough between the two peaks, which is the changeover instant -- at 15:00, the boundary of the conventional 07:00-15:00 / 15:00-23:00 pair, giving a 14:45-15:15 run. This is the weakest of the four authored hours and is the first one a site-specific configuration should override. It costs nothing today because nothing statistical reads the hour; it starts costing something the moment one does. DECISIONS.md section D244.

demandTemplates.name: Event egress template
demandTemplates.shape: near-zero baseline, then a step to a sustained one-way maximum, then decay
demandTemplates.$comment: A ballroom emptying, a cinema turning out, a floor of a conference breaking at once. THIS RECORD IS THE VENUE CASE AND ONLY THE VENUE CASE -- an office end-of-day is `office-down-peak`, a separate record, and until DECISIONS.md section D263 this one was doing both jobs while its comment argued only for this one. The shape differs from `rise-and-fall` in its LEADING EDGE rather than its magnitude: a rise-and-fall ramps, and an egress steps -- the doors open and the whole population is on the landing within a minute. That is the case a batch-window or deferred-assignment setting is decided by, and no shipped template produces it. DERIVED, not cited: the 20-minute duration, shorter than the other templates' 30 because an egress is over sooner and a longer window would dilute the peak the report is taken on. `peak-5min` is `rise-and-fall`'s own report window and is inherited. NOT CITED: the step's steepness and the decay rate; both are assumptions. LIMITATION: this template expresses the INTENSITY of an egress and not its ORIGIN. A real event egress leaves from one or two floors, and the directional split is a building-level property here rather than a per-floor one -- crown-hotel's 120-person ballroom is the concentration this template is meant to be run against, and pairing them is the caller's job. `packages/server/src/challenge/schedule.ts` is the shipped configuration that makes it, on crown-hotel; Free Play also offers this template in its list of every loaded record, so it is selectable besides. CLOCK (startOfDayMin 1344 = 22:24). NOT CITED, and this record's clock is now uncited END TO END rather than borrowing an office's citation: the sentence that stood here before section D263 read *CITED: that an end-of-day down-peak is a design case, and its demand level*, which was a citation for the OFFICE reading -- it has gone with that reading to `office-down-peak`, and nothing was left in its place, because no table in this project's reference set publishes an arrival rate or an hour for a venue turning out. CIBSE Guide D and ISO 8100-32 tabulate office design cases; an assembly space emptying is not one of them here. DERIVED, given the assumed 22:30: 22:24, by placing the template's HOLD rather than its start -- and for this shape the hold begins at the leading edge, which is the whole point of the template. Full flow is reached at durationMin/4 plus the 60-second step, i.e. +6 min, so a start of 22:24 puts the sustained maximum and the reported five minutes at 22:30-22:35, with the quiet trickle running from 22:24 and the decay ending at 22:44. NOT CITED: 22:30 itself, an assumption about when an evening function or a late screening turns out; it is section D244's own worked example (*a ballroom turning out at 22:30 is the same shape on a different clock*), promoted from a limitation to the record's authored hour now that the office reading has its own record. This is the weakest hour in the file after `shift-change`'s and is the second one a site-specific configuration should override. LIMITATION: the note above records that this template expresses the INTENSITY of an egress and not its ORIGIN, and the hour inherits that -- one clock cannot express both a matinee turning out and a midnight function. DECISIONS.md sections D244 and D263.

demandTemplates.name: Office down-peak template
demandTemplates.shape: ramp up to peak, hold, ramp down
demandTemplates.$comment: The office evening down-peak: the building emptying at the end of a working day. It exists because `evening-egress` was doing this job under a venue's name and a venue's comment, and one record cannot hold two clocks -- see DECISIONS.md section D263. The calendar's `quarter-end` period selects THIS record; `evening-egress` keeps the ballroom. CITED: that an office evening down-peak is a design case in its own right. It is one of the four office traffic types the reference set names alongside the morning up-peak, the lunch mixed peak and random interfloor traffic (Elevator World, *Fundamentals of Traffic Analysis*, cited in docs/02-elevator-reference.md's source list; CIBSE Guide D treats the same four). It is NOT an event egress under another name, which is the whole reason this record is not a copy of `evening-egress`'s numbers. NOT CITED, and stated plainly rather than filled in with a plausible figure: the down-peak's own ARRIVAL RATE. docs/03-traffic-and-statistics.md tabulates the office UP-peak at 11-15 %pop/5min (standard) and 15-17 % (prestige) and names it the governing peak; no page in this project's reference set gives a %pop/5min band for the office down-peak. The literature does say the evening flow is the more concentrated of the two, and that is exactly why quoting an unsourced multiple of the up-peak here would be the plausible-looking reference CLAUDE.md forbids. STRUCTURAL, and named so a reader does not go hunting: a `demandTemplates` record has NO rate field at all. The level a run is actually drawn at comes from the building's `arrivalRatePctPop5min` and the declared `traffic.demandLevel` parameter, and this record sets neither. What a template carries is the shape of demand over the period, not how much of it there is. DERIVED, not cited: every geometric number. The 30-minute duration, the 5-minute hold and the zero baseline are `rise-and-fall`'s own, inherited unchanged, so this record adds no uncited geometry -- the same discipline `lunch-two-way` and `shift-change` were authored under. LIMITATION, and it is the consequence of that inheritance: the shape is SYMMETRIC, and a real office down-peak is not. Departures synchronise at the front -- the working day ends at one time for most of the building -- and then trail long into the evening, so the true shape has a steeper rise than fall. Expressing that needs a skewed shape this module does not have and a skew figure no source here publishes, so it is neither cited nor modelled, and it is named here rather than implied by a symmetric ramp. CONSEQUENCE, measured rather than left to be discovered: because the geometry is `rise-and-fall`'s, a run of this template draws the SAME passengers as a run of `rise-and-fall` at the same seed -- `packages/core/src/traffic/templateAdditionIdentity.test.ts` asserts it on the legs. That is a declaration, not a defect: what this record adds is the hour and the period's identity, and section D244's rule 1 is that the hour moves nothing. A record that claimed a shape it did not have would be the section D112 defect; a record that says out loud which shape it shares is not. DIRECTION, and this record authors NONE: it declares no `directionalSplitAtStart`/`directionalSplitAtEnd`, deliberately. Those two fields are the model's way of saying *the mix MOVES within the run*, which is `lunch-two-way`'s arc and is not true of a down-peak -- a down-peak's mix is a level, not an arc -- and authoring a constant pair would also silently disable the calendar's own `splitBias`, which is where the shipped office down-peak's outgoing bias actually comes from. NOT CITED: the mix itself. The office down-peak's split is the morning up-peak's reversed -- roughly 5 incoming / 85 outgoing / 10 interfloor against the shipped `office-standard` profile's 85/5/10 -- and that is a statement of the mechanism (in the morning everyone rides up from the lobby; in the evening everyone rides down to it), not a quoted table. LIMITATION: because this record authors no mix, a run of it keeps each floor's own profile split unless the caller biases it, exactly as `evening-egress`'s ORIGIN limitation says of that shape; `quarter-end` biases 0.5 toward 0.1/0.8/0.1, which off an 85/5/10 office profile leaves incoming the LARGER share, and `packages/viz/src/shift/calendar.test.ts` already says so rather than claiming a down-peak it did not run. CLOCK (startOfDayMin 1035 = 17:15). NOT CITED: the hour. Guide D and ISO 8100-32 tabulate design PEAKS, not clocks. NOT CITED either: 17:30 itself, an assumption about when a working day ends -- it is the one figure carried over from `evening-egress`'s clock note, because it was always an assumption about an OFFICE and it belongs to this record. DERIVED: 17:15, by placing the template's HOLD rather than its start, the same derivation `rise-and-fall`'s 08:30 is. The hold is the reported five minutes and sits centred in the 30-minute run, at +12.5 to +17.5 min, so a start of 17:15 puts the reported peak at 17:27:30-17:32:30, centred on 17:30. Read the pair together: the same building's day opens at 08:30 for a peak at 08:45 and closes at 17:15 for a peak at 17:30. LIMITATION: as for `rise-and-fall`, the derivation is a function of durationMin and of the 5-minute hold, so changing either leaves 17:15 no longer centring the hold on 17:30, and nothing in the code will say so. Nothing statistical reads startOfDayMin today -- intensityAt, splitAt and integratedIntensityS never see it -- so the assumption is free, and it stops being free the moment a phase boundary becomes a measurement boundary. DECISIONS.md sections D244 and D263.

passengerMass.$comment: Drives the load sensor. Must be a distribution, not a constant, or the load sensor has nothing to measure.
